examTip: Development is not just about money. Use economic AND social measures together, and say why each one can mislead.
introTips: Know at least two economic measures (GNI per head) and two social measures (life expectancy, infant mortality rate).
The HDI combines income, life expectancy and education into one score.
Causes of uneven development come in three groups: physical, economic and historical.
intro: In Japan, about 2 babies in every 1,000 die before their first birthday. In Nigeria it is about 70 in every 1,000. Why are some countries so much richer and healthier than others? This lesson shows how geographers measure development, why the gap between countries exists, what it leads to, and how people try to close it.

basics.text: Quality of life means how good people's lives are. It includes having enough food, clean water, a home, health care and school.
Income is the money a person or a country earns. A higher income usually means people can buy more of what they need.
"Per person" means shared out equally between everyone. If 100 sweets are shared by 4 people, that is 25 sweets per person.
Trade is buying and selling between countries. Selling goods to another country is exporting. Buying goods from another country is importing.
A debt is money that is owed. A country that borrows money must pay it back. It often pays extra on top, called interest.
Poverty means not having enough money for basic needs. These are things like food, clean water and a home.

keyPoints.heading: What is development and how do we measure it?
keyPoints.content: Development means people's quality of life getting better: richer, healthier and better educated. To compare countries, geographers use measures. Economic measures are about money. The main one is GNI per head (gross national income per head): all the income a country earns in a year, divided by its number of people. In 2025 it was about $88,810 in the USA, $54,550 in the UK, $1,360 in Nigeria and $750 in Niger. Social measures are about people's lives. Life expectancy is how long a baby born now can expect to live: about 84 years in Japan and 55 in Nigeria. The infant mortality rate is how many babies in every 1,000 born alive die before their first birthday. Others are birth and death rates, people per doctor, the literacy rate (the share of adults who can read and write) and access to safe water. Birth, death and infant mortality rates are always "per 1,000" each year: per 1,000 people, or per 1,000 babies born alive. The literacy rate is different: it is a percentage. The HDI (Human Development Index) combines three things into one score between 0 and 1: income, life expectancy and education. Every measure has limitations: reasons it can mislead. GNI per head is an average, so it hides how unequally money is shared. Birth rates are affected by religion and culture, not only by development. Data from poorer countries can be out of date or guessed. One measure on its own never gives the whole picture.
writeBullets: Development: quality of life getting better, in money and in people's lives
Economic measure: GNI per head, a country's yearly income divided by its population
Social measures: life expectancy, infant mortality rate, birth and death rates, people per doctor, literacy, safe water
Birth, death and infant mortality rates: per 1,000 each year; literacy rate: a percentage
HDI: one score from income, life expectancy and education
Limitation = why a measure can mislead: an average hides inequality; birth rates depend on culture too

keyTerms.def: Gross national income per head: all the income a country earns in a year, divided by the number of people living there. It is an average income for each person.
The average number of years a baby born now in a country can expect to live.
The number of babies, out of every 1,000 born alive, who die before their first birthday, in a year.
Human Development Index: one score between 0 and 1 that combines income, life expectancy and education. Close to 1 means rich, long-lived and well educated.
A reason a measure can give a misleading picture, such as an average hiding big differences between rich and poor people.

keyPoints.memTip: GNI counts the cash; HDI adds health and learning.
keyPoints.tutor_note: A limitation answer must say why the measure can mislead, not just what it leaves out.

keyPoints.heading: Ways of classifying countries
keyPoints.content: Countries can be grouped by their level of development. The World Bank is an international organisation that lends money for development. It groups countries by GNI per head. HICs (high income countries) include the UK and Japan. LICs (low income countries) include Niger and Malawi. In between are middle income countries, split into upper-middle and lower-middle. Kenya is lower-middle income: still a poorer country, with a GNI per head of $2,200 in 2025. NEEs (newly emerging economies) are countries whose economies have started to grow fast as they build up industry, such as China, India, Brazil and Nigeria. An older way of dividing the world is the Brandt Line, drawn on a map to separate a richer "North" from a poorer "South". It fits today's world badly: some countries in the "South", such as China, now have some of the world's largest economies.
keyPoints.diagramCaption: The Brandt Line: a rough split between a richer North and a poorer South.
writeBullets: World Bank groups by GNI per head: HICs, upper-middle and lower-middle income countries, LICs; Kenya is lower-middle income
NEEs: economies growing fast as industry builds up (China, India, Brazil, Nigeria)
Brandt Line: richer North, poorer South; out of date because of fast-growing NEEs

keyTerms.def: High income country: a wealthy country with a high GNI per head, such as the UK or Japan.
Low income country: one of the world's poorest countries, with a low GNI per head, such as Niger.
Newly emerging economy: a country whose economy has started to grow fast as it builds up industry, such as Nigeria, India or Brazil.
A line drawn on a world map to split a richer North from a poorer South. It is a rough guide that fits today's world badly.
An international organisation that lends money to countries for development, and groups countries by their income.

keyPoints.memTip: HIC at the top, LIC at the bottom; NEEs are the fast movers in between.
keyPoints.tutor_note: Saying why the Brandt Line is out of date earns evaluation marks.

keyPoints.heading: Population and development: the Demographic Transition Model
keyPoints.content: As a country develops, its births and deaths change in a pattern. The Demographic Transition Model (DTM) shows this pattern in five stages. It compares the birth rate (births for every 1,000 people each year) with the death rate (deaths for every 1,000 people each year). Stage 1: both rates are high, so the population stays small. Few places are like this today. Stage 2: the death rate falls fast as clean water, food and health care improve, but the birth rate stays high. The population grows fast. Many LICs are here. Stage 3: the birth rate falls too, as fewer babies die, more girls go to school and more women go out to work. Growth slows. Many NEEs are here. Stage 4: both rates are low and the population is steady. Most HICs, such as the UK, are here. Stage 5: the birth rate falls below the death rate and the population shrinks slowly, as in Japan. So a country's stage in the DTM gives a clue to its level of development. Moving into stage 3 can help the economy: with fewer children to look after, more women can work.
writeBullets: DTM: birth and death rates change in five stages as a country develops
Stage 2: death rate falls, birth rate high, fast growth: many LICs
Stage 3: birth rate falls too (fewer babies die, girls' schooling, women working): many NEEs
Stage 4: both low, steady population: most HICs
Stage 5: births below deaths, population shrinks (Japan)
Stage 3 can boost the economy: more women able to work

keyTerms.def: A model with five stages showing how a country's birth and death rates, and so its population, change as it develops.
The number of babies born for every 1,000 people in a year.
The number of people who die for every 1,000 people in a year.

keyPoints.memTip: Deaths drop first, births follow: that is the transition.
keyPoints.tutor_note: Link each stage to a level of development with one example.

keyPoints.heading: Uneven development: causes and consequences
keyPoints.content: Development is uneven: some countries are much further ahead than others. The difference between the richest and poorest countries is called the development gap. Its causes come in three groups. Physical causes come from nature. A landlocked country, with no coastline, pays more to trade. Poor soils, drought and natural hazards such as floods or earthquakes damage farming and buildings. Diseases such as malaria keep people from working. Economic causes come from trade and money. Many poorer countries sell raw materials such as coffee or copper, called primary products, which earn little and whose prices change a lot. They buy costly manufactured goods. Paying back debts leaves less money for schools and hospitals. Historical causes come from the past. Under colonialism, European countries ruled much of Africa and Asia, taking raw materials and drawing borders that split peoples. Uneven development has consequences. There are big disparities (differences) in wealth and in health. It also causes international migration: people move from poorer countries to richer ones for work, higher pay and safety. Many send money home to their families.
keyPoints.diagramCaption: Causes of the development gap, each feeding the others.
writeBullets: Physical causes: landlocked, poor soils, drought, natural hazards, disease
Economic causes: selling cheap primary products, buying costly goods, debt
Historical causes: colonialism took raw materials and drew borders that split peoples
Consequences: disparities in wealth and health
Consequence: international migration from poorer to richer countries for work and pay; money sent home

keyTerms.def: The difference in wealth and quality of life between the richest and the poorest countries.
Raw materials sold before anything is made from them, such as crops, oil or metal ores. They earn far less than manufactured goods.
When one country rules another and runs it for its own benefit, as European countries did in much of Africa and Asia.
People moving from one country to live in another, often from poorer countries to richer ones for work and higher pay.

keyPoints.memTip: Physical, economic, historical: nature, money, the past.
keyPoints.tutor_note: For a physical cause, name something natural: landlocked, drought, hazards, disease.

keyPoints.heading: Strategies to reduce the development gap
keyPoints.content: Several strategies try to close the gap. Investment: companies or other countries put money into businesses, roads and factories. Industrial development creates jobs and taxes. Aid is help from one country or charity to another: money, goods or skills, given or lent on very easy terms. Emergency aid helps after a disaster; long-term aid pays for schools or wells. It can be wasted or make a country depend on it. Intermediate technology is simple equipment local people can make, use and mend, such as a hand water pump. Fairtrade pays farmers a fair minimum price, plus extra money for their community. Debt relief cancels some of a poor country's debt, so money paid out as interest can go on health and schools instead. Under one international scheme, most of the 39 poor countries that qualified have had much of their debt cancelled. Microfinance means very small loans to people too poor to use an ordinary bank, to start a business. Grameen Bank in Bangladesh lends mostly to women. Tourism brings money and jobs. In Kenya, a poorer country that is growing fast, tourism has grown: about 1.2 million international tourists came in 2015 and about 2 million in 2019, for safaris and beaches. In 2019 tourism earned $1.76 billion, about 15% of what Kenya earns from selling abroad. That money pays wages, taxes and new roads. But much of it can go to foreign hotel companies, and visitor numbers fall after terrorism or a pandemic.
writeBullets: Investment and industrial development: jobs and taxes
Aid: emergency or long-term; can be wasted or create dependence
Intermediate technology: simple kit locals can make and mend
Fairtrade: fair minimum price plus money for the community
Debt relief: cancelled debt frees money for health and schools; most of the 39 countries that qualified have been helped
Microfinance: tiny loans to start businesses; Grameen Bank lends mostly to women
Tourism in Kenya: visitors grew from about 1.2 million (2015) to 2 million (2019); $1.76 billion, 15% of exports; jobs and taxes, but money can leak abroad

keyTerms.def: Help from one country or organisation to another: money, goods or skills, given or lent on very easy terms, either after a disaster or for long-term projects.
A scheme that pays farmers a fair minimum price for their crop, plus extra money for their community.
Cancelling part or all of the money a poor country owes, so it can spend that money on its own people.
Simple, cheap equipment that local people can make, use and repair themselves.
Very small loans to people too poor to use an ordinary bank, usually to start a small business.

keyPoints.memTip: Aid gives, debt relief forgives, microfinance lends.
keyPoints.tutor_note: Debt relief is not a loan: it cancels what is owed. Microfinance is a loan.

keyPoints.heading: Is the development gap closing?
keyPoints.content: The picture is mixed. Some NEEs, especially China and India, have grown fast, and hundreds of millions of their people now have higher incomes. Across the world, the share of people in extreme poverty (living on less than $3 a day) fell from about 43% in 1990 to about 10% in 2024. But progress is uneven. Many of the poorest countries, especially in Africa south of the Sahara, are falling further behind. The United Nations has set Sustainable Development Goals, targets for every country to end poverty and hunger and improve health and schooling.
writeBullets: Some NEEs (China, India) closing the gap fast
Extreme poverty (under $3 a day): about 43% of people in 1990, about 10% in 2024
Many of the poorest African countries falling further behind
Sustainable Development Goals: UN targets on poverty, hunger, health, schooling

keyTerms.def: Living on less than the international poverty line, now $3 a day: too little for basic food, shelter and health care.
Targets agreed at the United Nations for every country, covering poverty, hunger, health, education and the environment.
Newly emerging economy: a country whose economy has started to grow fast as it builds up industry, such as Nigeria, India or Brazil.

keyPoints.memTip: Closing for the fast growers, widening for many of the poorest.
keyPoints.tutor_note: A judgement needs evidence for both sides.

0.question: Why is the HDI a better measure of development than GNI per head on its own?
options: It combines income, life expectancy and education, so it shows more about people's lives
It only uses money data, which is more reliable
It measures one country over time instead of comparing countries
It counts how many people live in a country
0.correctFeedback: Right. The HDI brings together income, health and education, so a country cannot score high just by being rich.
0.wrongFeedback: Not quite. The HDI combines income, life expectancy and education. GNI per head only shows money, not whether people live long, healthy, educated lives.

3.question: Which of these is a physical cause of uneven development?
options: Being landlocked, with no coastline, so trade costs more
Selling cheap raw materials and buying costly goods
3.correctFeedback: Right. Being landlocked comes from geography, so it is a physical cause.
3.wrongFeedback: Not quite. Debts and trade are economic causes; colonial borders are historical. Being landlocked is physical: it comes from where the country is.

commonMistakes: Giving a limitation of a measure as what it does not show. Say why it can mislead: GNI per head is an average, so it hides how unequally money is shared.
Saying a rate without "per 1,000 per year". The infant mortality rate is babies dying before their first birthday for every 1,000 born alive, each year.
Confusing debt relief with a loan. Debt relief cancels money owed; microfinance is a small loan.
Mixing up aid with microfinance, tourism or TNCs. Aid is help from governments or charities: gifts, or loans on very easy terms. It is not a business earning a profit.
Not knowing what a physical cause is. It comes from nature: being landlocked, drought, hazards, disease.
Confusing infant mortality rate with life expectancy.
examTips: For a limitation question, give one reason the measure can mislead and explain it.
For causes, use the three groups: physical, economic and historical, each with an example.
When judging tourism, use a named country: Kenya earned $1.76 billion from tourism in 2019, but some money leaks to foreign companies.
For a judgement question ("Do you agree?"), give evidence for both sides from a named example, then say which side is stronger and why.
